samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Chartley M. Morley was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. Here we are on September 27th, 2002 in Spokane, Washington at the National 4th Infantry Division reunion sitting in a DoubleTree Hotel. And I am talking to Chartley M. Morley of [address redacted]. Chartley was born in Bartlesville, Oklahoma on January 10th, 1920. She served in the United States Army in the Women's Medical Service Corps, and we'll let her --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: All right. Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Specialist Corps.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Specialist Corps, okay. And we'll let her talk about this. My name is Bob Babcock. I represent Americans Remembered, and I am interviewing for the Veterans History Project to go into the National Archives. I have known Chartley since 1965 when I served under the command of her husband, Len Morley, and Chartley in 1st Battalion 22nd Infantry at Fort Lewis, Washington prior to going to Vietnam. So now what we'll do is we'll talk. Chartley, you were born in Bartlesville, Oklahoma, [birthdate redacted]. How long did you live there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Till I was two-and-a-half.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Till you were two-and-a-half. Then where did you go?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: We moved to Tulsa.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Tulsa, okay. How long were you in Tulsa?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Till I was 13.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: To California; Oakland, California.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Oakland. So you were one of the Okies going to --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: That's for sure.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: All right. During the Depression.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Very much in the Depression, 1933.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. All right. All right. Do you remember that trip?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Indeed, I do.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How was it?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, I had spent the summer in North Platte with my sister. My father was in California. He had gotten a job, and my mother and brother were in Bartlesville with my older brother. And my younger brother and I had never been separated really. Like all siblings, we had our disagreements, but we swore to our mother that if we just got together one more time, we'd never fight again. And we met, it was arranged that they would go by train, as I would from North Platte, they would go from Tulsa, and we would meet in Cheyenne where the trains met, and we would go to California. We arrived in the middle of the night. We were met by my father and my cousin's husband and taken to their home where I was put in bed with my cousin in the middle of the night, and she wasn't very receptive to someone in her bed. It was a very difficult move for me in that I came from a situation where there wasn't -- Everyone was hurting being because of the Depression, and this community where we went was a very prosperous community -- Leonard Morley: Upscale.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: -- and very upscale. It was -- the small community was surrounded by the city of Oakland, it was Piedmont, and they had their schools. Here I was an Okie with an accent, and I was ahead of myself in school. I was in the 10th grade at age 13. And they had gone to school with one another from kindergarten, and I was the outsider. I was a very unhappy young woman.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Very unhappy. Let me ask you a question. Chartley, I've never heard that name before. Tell me the -- about Chartley. I've always wondered about that.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I was named for my grandmother --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: -- who was born in Chicago in 1842. It's an English name, and there is a town in Massachusetts by the name of Chartley which Len and I visited, and the postmaster sent me a letter addressed to me with the postmark.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Neat.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And about a year later he sent me a brochure, they at that time which would have been in 1961 or 2, he sent me a brochure where they celebrated their 250th anniversary.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That's neat. That's a great -- I've always wondered about that. I've known you since 1965 and never knew where that came from. Okay. So you went to a suburb of Oakland at 13 years old, and you stayed there until you were grown?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, we then moved from my cousin's home to our own home. And my younger brother and I, we both had jobs, and I started at the University of California at age 16. And I graduated from Oakland High.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And I did five years at the university with a certificate. At that time there were 60 hospitals in the United States that were accredited to the American Dietetic Association of which the university was one.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you were -- you earned a degree as a dietitian?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum. I had a year's internship at the hospital.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. And what year was that that you graduated?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Actually I would have been -- Well, I got my certificate in '41.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: 1941. So tell me where you were on December 7th, 1941.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I know it well.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: I bet you do.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I had been married in September of that year, and because until the 1st of December I was at the hospital working broken shifts in San Francisco. The 1st of December I was in the clinic then, so we had regular hours, and in January I was coming back to the campus at Berkeley. So we got an apartment because my husband had worked for this man taking care of rental properties while he was in school, and he said if we would clean this apartment, we could have it. Of course, housing was very much at a premium because of the shipyard starting to work.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: This precluded our being able to go out, and we certainly couldn't afford it, that we got this apartment. And I was on my hands and knees scrubbing the floor in the kitchen, small kitchen, when it came on the radio.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: What did you do? Did you keep scrubbing or did you --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I kept scrubbing. Life changed that day.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And my husband had --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: What was your husband's name?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Nels (phonetic) Shugren, S-h-u-g-r-e-n.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: He had been one of the first classes at Pensacola that was reduced in the length of service before they got their wings. He was number one man in the class and had one month left to graduate when his eyes gave out, and at that point they were washing them out without really any cause but, of course, landing planes on a carrier was much different then than it is today.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And he was sent home.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And that would have been what year now?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: '40 that he came home.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So this was before Pearl Harbor, he was in. Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yes. And then he went to work. In the meantime he took an exam to be a navigator for the Air Corps and didn't hear from them. And in December -- This was in December when Pearl Harbor came along and, of course, that just made him all the more anxious to join the service, and so early January he volunteered to go to the Marine Academy -- Merchant Marine Academy, I should say.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And I said goodbye to him, and that evening I came out of the hospital and there he was. He had gone to the draft board to tell them he was leaving, and they said Sorry, you're being drafted. Well, he was drafted and went to Fort Ord, and from there he went to Camp Callan in southern California. Because of his experience in the Navy and his ROTC experience at Berkeley, they wanted him to go to OCS, and he was scheduled to do that when the Air Corps decided they wanted him.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: He was discharged from the Army and went to the Air Corps and subsequently received his wings as a navigator.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: As a navigator on what type of an aircraft?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, they were flying just about anything.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Anything.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And he was sent to St. Joe, Missouri and from there to Wilmington, Delaware.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Where were you during this time?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I was working in San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you were staying back continuing to work in a hospital?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: In a hospital. I was the first full-time dietitian at Hahnemann Hospital in San Francisco. Then I just decided that he couldn't be by himself, and I resigned and left on the 1st of March in 1943 to go and join him in Wilmington. At that time he left on a flight ferrying supplies to the Russians in Afghanistan.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: But, of course, there was no transcontinental flights at that point, and this was in an A-20. And they went down through the Caribbean, Trinidad, into Brazil, and he was lost off the coast of Brazil.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: They ever recover anything?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Never recovered anything. So this was, would have been what date?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Let's see. March the 20th.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: March 20th, 1943?

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How long before you got the word?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I was in Wilmington, and I was staying with a pilot's wife. I had gotten an apartment, but I was staying at night with this lady who she was a pilot's wife, and on the entry hall table there was a notice that I had a telegram. And we were expecting the men back, so I just assumed that it was notice that they were coming, and I called -- It was a postal telegraph, and I called and asked if they would read it. And they said they were too busy to read it. They would send it out to me. And this little, she couldn't have been more than 12 years old, black girl, came to the door. And she knew what it was and handed me this. And I went to get something to pay her, and she vanished. And that's how I found out.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That's how you found out. Did you keep that telegram?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I did.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. You still have it?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I have it.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Could we get a copy of it?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Oh, if I can find it.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: If you can find it. That would be interesting to put in the archives. So at 23 years old you're a widow.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: What do you do now?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, I went back -- It was difficult for my family to get me back to California. I didn't want to go. And my sister's husband was a lieutenant commander in the Navy and was in Washington, and he had orders for San Francisco. And he called me and said I want you to go to South Dakota and drive your sister and their two daughters to California, which I did. But made arrangements to go to work the day after I got there, but it was a temporary job. I worked in a cannery. I did bookkeeping and personnel work and cost accounting and all that.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And then the hospital called me and wanted me to come back, which I did, and of course at that point you didn't make any decision about what you wanted to do with your life. And at the end of the year at that point they were -- those that were missing were declared legally dead. And as I only wanted to serve my country and be patriotic and I could be commissioned because of my education and background, I was commissioned in August of '44.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: August of '44.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: But at that point I must say that prior to World War II the women in the Women's Medical Specialist Corps were civilians, and in '42 they were given temporary commissions because they couldn't be sent overseas as a civilian during the war years.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: In 1947 after the war was over they were made a special corps which was within the medical department. It since has become the Medical Specialist Corps because they have men, PT, physical therapists, and so forth.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Now, did you get any insurance from the government?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: $50 a month.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: $50 a month. Okay. So August 1944 you are commissioned as a second lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: $125 a month.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: $125 was good money back then, wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: But not really, right?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Where were you -- where was -- what was your first duty assignment?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I was assigned to Camp White, Oregon where we went to basic training, and we learned to take apart field ranges and use dehydrated foods because we didn't know where we would be assigned. While I was there the whole unit was transferred to Fort Lewis, Washington where we learned to march, the slit trenches and bivouac. And from there I went when we finished with the basic, I was sent to the city of San Francisco and was there only temporarily until I was reassigned to Fort Lewis with the 220th General Hospital.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Did you get any weapons training?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Not as such, no. We did not carry weapons.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So by --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: We wore Red Cross armbands.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So by the time you got to the 220th General Hospital at Fort Lewis, what month and year was it?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: The end of September.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: End of September '44?

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So what happened there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, it was interesting in that they were staging, and the only -- There were three women assigned to the hospital. It was a General Hospital. There were no -- there were no nurses available as such, and so they had extra corpsmen. And we left Fort Lewis bound for the European theater in January.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: January of '45?

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Now, why did they send you to Europe instead of to the Pacific since you're sitting on the Pacific coast?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, that's a good question.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: But there were three women on board the troop train going to Boston.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you took a troop train from San Francisco --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No. From Fort Lewis.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: From Fort Lewis to Boston. Any interesting things come to mind from the troop train trip?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Oh, yes. Of course, there was not fraternization or anything like there is today or cohabitation, shall I say, within the barracks. And I don't mean living together, but men and women in the same barracks. And the Pullman people were very protective of the women that were on their trains. We were assigned, even though we were all -- the three of us were officers, we were sort of low man on the totem pole as far as the doctors and the staff were concerned. But the Pullman people, they refused to let us -- because they had taken curtains off of the Pullman cars, we couldn't be in the troop trains, and so three officers were discommoded, and we were given their state room with doors -- with a door.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And the first morning after we left Fort Lewis there was a rap on our door and here were three soldiers with three trays for our breakfast. Because the mess car was next to the engine, and we would have had to go through all the troop train cars, and the men would have had to be in uniform, so we got our breakfast served to us every morning.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How long did it take you to make that trip?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: It was quite a while.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you got to Boston.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And it was cold.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And we're January 1945. So what happens when you get to Boston?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, procedure was that we were all to march to our quarters in full field pack, helmet, helmet liner, full canteen, gas mask, the whole bit. And it was bitter cold, but the sun was shining, lots of snow. And as we came off of the train, the loudspeaker system said All female personnel stand aside and wait transportation. And we had so many friends who wanted, will you take this, because they didn't want to carry their bed rolls or their field packs. Anyhow, but we were billeted there, and from there we went to -- we were joined by two physical therapists and five Red Cross women.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So by now you're up to ten.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Ten women.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Ten women, 220th Field General Hospital.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: January '45 in Boston, and you're en route to Europe.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So when did you -- How did you get to Europe?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: We went on a ship, and there were ten women on the ship. It was -- our billets -- it was a rather small ship, I think the Patrick Henry if I remember right, and when they had drills, when the abandon ship would sound and we'd have drills, there was not room in the day room and everything for all the people. So they would just tell us to stay in our quarters, and they would make sure we were rescued. The morning we were to have landed in Le Havre, but about 4:30, 5:00 in the morning there was a tremendous concussion, and our ship was hit with another ship in the channel in heavy, heavy fog. They didn't have radar as they have today. And so everyone sat still and, of course, the channel was heavily mined, and eventually they took us to Southampton, and we stayed on the ship. Fortunately, no one was hurt, but the deck was split, the steel deck was split about 20 feet in. And then the next morning we -- as all soldiers know, you get up at o-dark-thirty and get ready and then you wait all day, which we did. And finally about 4:30 in the afternoon, and it was getting dark, they came with a two-and-a-half ton truck to take us to a staging area. Only the five of us, the five military women went. The Red Cross women went to Paris for orientation. And we went to a place that was called Menier, and it was near Dieppe.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Time out. How did you get from England to --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: On the same ship.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. Same ship went, so you didn't change ships.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. Even though it was damaged, you went on with it.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: It didn't interfere with its --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: -- mobility.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So you were in Dieppe.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, we were actually near Rouen, but we took a side trip eventually to Dieppe one day.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: All right. And by now it's when? What's the month?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, the end of January.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: End of January '45. So the Bulge is over, and we're back regaining the offensive heading across into Germany. So where'd you go from there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: There we set up our hospital in Suippes-sur-Marne which is outside of Reims.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And it was in an old French military place. The Germans had occupied it at one time. And this was the rear echelon staging area for the 82nd Airborne before their last push-off. And the five women, military women, we set up without nurses, and most of our patients had gone through Italy and North Africa, and we had a lot of men who had been prisoners, and there were -- Of course, transporting of food and supplies was not like it is today. There was not the refrigeration. There was not the capacity of the ships or the staging -- storing of things, so that our rations were somewhat limited, but we did the best we could. And we used -- because American soldiers were limited in the number that we had, and we had some wonderful Italian boys from the Pennsylvania area and Ohio, I never will forget them, and we used German PWs in the mix, and it was a privilege for them. So we had from old sergeants to very young boys, but we never had any problems. The only problem we had was because of scarcity of rations sometimes and when a man had not eaten properly from being in prison, his eyes were often larger than his stomach, and he had to have -- so one of us -- the other two ladies with me, one was Edith Yocella (phonetic) and Mabel Walker. Edith was from California, and Mabel was from Oklahoma. And one of us was always there so that if a server, meaning a German prisoner, said the man couldn't have seconds, we could always kid them and say If you're really hungry, you come back and see me. And usually they didn't want. But one of the things we did that was fun, and I've often wondered if anyone ever remembered, and that was we had taken -- each of us had taken a small hot plate, and the men that had been prisoners, and most of them were not ambulatory, they wanted fried eggs. Well, our eggs were not always the freshest, but we took our mess kits, and we'd do one at a time, and we fried eggs for those prisoners that wanted them. So I've often wondered if anyone ever thought about that.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: These were primarily American prisoners --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: -- that had been captured during Africa.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And Italy.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And Italy, okay. They had been liberated by American troops. What was your uniform?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: What was our uniform?

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yeah, what was your uniform?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: We had a Seersucker, brown-and-white stripe Seersucker slacks and sort of a wraparound dress. We wore fatigues. We had combat -- we had boots. We had four-buckle arctic galoshes and women's winter woolies that were issued at Fort Lewis. Leonard Morley: You had the OD uniform.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: The ODs.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yeah. Did you -- did you ever have any buzz bombs or German bombers or anything that you had to contend with?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, they always called it, what was it, Midnight Charlie.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Bed Check Charlie.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: That went -- We were aware of that. And, of course, the Airborne practiced their jumps right outside the hospital there. And this was -- we really didn't have a lot of air activity over us because we weren't near an air base really.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: That I was aware of.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you're now -- you're in the winter of 1945. The war is going well after the Battle of the Bulge. Are you getting more casualties other than PWs or are you getting --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You're getting all kinds.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum. But a lot of it was minor, but they were in the stage of going -- going back to maybe England for further treatment or back to the States.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How about did you get any German prisoners, did you treat any of those?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Only the ones that worked for us. One day the sergeant came to me and he said Lieutenant, can you do something? It was the youngest one that they had, and he was sort of everyone's favorite, and he had a toothache, and he was really suffering, and so we went to the dentist. They took care of that. Otherwise we really didn't have a lot of problems with them.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: But you were a stabilized hospital. You didn't move. You stayed in the same spot.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And how long did you stay in that spot?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, V-E Day came not too long after that, and then because we were a new unit over there, we were designated to go to the CBI by way of the Suez Canal.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: What's the CBI?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: China-Burma-India.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: China-Burma-India, okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Just should say the Far East but through the canal and get to the East by that. So our hospital, all new equipment and everything, there were two General Hospitals in the same area that were brand new really, and all of that equipment was turned over to the French, and we were staged and went from that area to Marseille, and then V-J Day came along.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Before we go along, let's back up to V-E Day. Tell me about V-E Day, how did -- where were you, how did you react, what was your reaction to that?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: When I heard -- heard about it, it was a bright sunny day as I remember, and I went outside the mess hall, and I walked around and I cried.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: What -- how did you feel? Did you feel like you had done your part?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, I hoped I had.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yup.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And then we had a parade. I still have the little flags that -- Of course, there were no -- people didn't have anything, and I drew the unlucky or maybe it was lucky, I don't know, straw that I stayed on duty and the other two marched in the parade in the little town of Suippes. And the French had made out of scraps of material they'd sewn red, white and blue French flags. And I still have one in my scrap book.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Let me -- let me stop again. Now, the two ladies you were with, are you still in touch with them?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No, not -- I saw both of them after the service, and Edith [sic] stayed in Washington, D.C. She worked for the Department of Agriculture. And Edith was in California. And while I was still in California after the war, I saw her occasionally, and we had dinner together. But I have not kept in touch with them, unfortunately. They were both a little older than I, and now at age 83 I don't know if they're still living or not.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So let's go on up. You're ready to go to China-Burma-India, V-J Day, Victory in Japan happens, and you're still sitting in the hospital. You've turned everything over to the French. What are you doing?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, no, we were in Marseille.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You're in Marseille. What are you doing in Marseille?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, our hospital -- we were in a staging area and waiting to go when the -- and had our money exchanged as I remember for -- and then they decided rather than go around through the canal, that they would send one of the -- There were two hospitals in Marseille, General Hospitals, and that one would stay and one would go. And ours was slated to come home through the States and then deploy. We had a lot of nurses by that time that had been levied from hospitals, and many of them had been there for a long time, and the doctors that had gone with us, a lot of them were older men that, you know, on more or less short tours. And so it was to be reorganized and then sent to the Far East through the States.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And our money had been exchanged and we were ready, we were packed ready to go, and the other hospital's commander decided that their hospital should go. So here we were sitting with very disgruntled people, and there was a need for a hospital in Marseille. It was not a very pleasant situation in that supplies were -- they weren't shipping a lot of things, so we were using things that had been stockpiled. And we -- it was the hospital for the disciplinary barracks in Marseille in which we had probably 250 patients from there.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Again, these are American troops?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: GIs, and they were -- most of them were ambulatory, so they came to the mess hall, and this presented problems. It was also a hospital where they had a very large ward area that was used for VD patients, and this was not a pleasant assignment. And where our billets were, we were in an old house, chateau down the street, and water wasn't potable even and that sort of thing, but we managed.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How long did you do that? You went from, what, this was August or so, September of '45, and how long did you do that?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, we didn't get there -- we got there earlier. See, we were there for V-E Day -- I mean V-J Day.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: V-J Day, yeah.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And from -- I got orders to go to Salzburg, Austria in August, the latter part of August.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Salzburg, what were you going to do there, another hospital?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: What was the hospital's number? Leonard Morley: 124th.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yeah, 124th.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: 124th General Hospital.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: General Hospital.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. In Salzburg, Austria. So you went down there in August?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And you have the same job?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, the person I was to replace, she hadn't gotten orders yet. So then I was sent on temporary duty to a field hospital down on the Oder Sea where they were having difficulties with rations and feeding the patients adequately and the staff. Because we were at that time there was an organization called UNRRA that the American government was funding and supporting, and they ate in our messes, and so we had a large number that we fed, but the supplies were limited.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And so I went there on temporary duty until they needed me in Salzburg. And I was there until the end of November, and then I went to Salzburg. Leonard Morley: Tell him about your --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So 19 -- November 1945 you're back in Salzburg, right? Is that right?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You were in the temporary field office. Okay. So November of '45 you take over as the dietitian in the 124th General Hospital. Do you want to go home? I mean, the war's over.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No. Well, I was doing my duty and my time. I still had my time to do.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: A soldier is a soldier, right.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum. But then I got orders to go home in February I guess it was, and in March I came home.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: February of '46?

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: March '46 you came home. Now, between the time you got there in '45, in November '45, and March '46, did anything happen in your life that had a long-term impact on it?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, I met Leonard Morley, but he was everyone's friend.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Leonard Morley, who's that?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And he had transportation.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And none of us gals had any transportation, and he was just kind to everybody.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: This was this dashing young infantry lieutenant from the 42nd Infantry Division who was now assigned to what type of a job?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I think he was in the prison. Leonard Morley: War crimes -- war crimes prison.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: War crimes prison, where they were discharging soldiers.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. Okay. So you've got a war crimes lieutenant who has made his mark as a combat infantryman in the 42nd Infantry Division, and he's got transportation. So did you just sit in the car and let him transport you or was there anything else involved there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No. He'd call and ask if you'd like to go to the movie or something, and you'd say Oh, fine. And then you'd go to your room after duty and change your clothes, and the phone would ring and they'd say Lieutenant Shugren, you have a caller. And you go down and he would have called two or three gals, and we all went to the movie. But he also had a Newfoundland dog, Leo, that sat in the rear of the jeep, and I think that was his protection.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Protecting him from all the women, huh? I'm sure he needed that. Okay. So I mean he was going off, he's dating everybody.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: But see, he sang to all of us.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That's right. I've heard him sing. What did he sing?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: There wasn't a song he didn't know. All of them. Semi-classics and the musicals and just all the songs.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. Now, when did it get to the stage where he quit inviting the whole crew and he started only inviting you?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Never.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Never?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So he had group dates. Did he ever bring any friends along?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, they usually came and would meet -- We'd go to the Bischofshofen [sic], and we ate C-rations in style and had lovely music and danced and --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Didn't drink any beer or drink any wine, did you?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You didn't?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I didn't.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You didn't. All right.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: That wasn't part of life then.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yup. Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And then I came home. At the same time, how it happened I don't know, but we -- Edith was stationed in Vienna and Mabel was stationed in Munich, and we all ended up on the same orders, and we all came home together.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How did you come home? On a boat?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Certainly. There was not air transportation in those days.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And so Edith came to Salzburg, and then we went by train to Munich, and we picked up -- and Mabel joined us, and we ended up in Le Havre.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. And you came home, you came back into what, New York?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: What happened when you got to New York? Now, let's see, we're March '46, right, March 1946. Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you get to New York harbor.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: What was your reaction when you got back to the States?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, we were all out there on the deck watching for the Statue of Liberty, and it had been a rough crossing. We had rough storms, and we were glad to be there. Went from there to Kilmer, Camp Kilmer, and waited transportation. They were flying those that came into the east coast and lived on the west coast, they were flown. It was a shuttle. And those that came in on the west coast that lived on the east coast, they'd just -- C-147, bucket seats.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you flew back to Oakland?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And went to see your family?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: That was interesting in that we arrived in Oakland probably 4:00 in the morning or something like that, and there were no facilities. There were eight women on that plane, and there were no facilities for females at the Oakland Army Base. So they were going to transport us back to San Francisco. And as two of us were from Oakland, we asked if we could go home. We were just a couple miles from home, three miles maybe, four. And so they took a 45-passenger bus and they said we all had to stay together, and Edith called her parents, I called mine and said we're bringing -- each of us took three for breakfast and had breakfast. And then they allowed me to take my little '37 Ford, and I could drive it. We had to go to Marysville, which is up north of Sacramento, for discharge. And so I took three gals in my little '37 Ford and away we went.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you're 26 years old now, and you go up -- And this is still March '46?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And you go up to around Sacramento.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Camp Beale.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Camp Beale, and you get discharged. Do you have any idea what you're going to do next?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I didn't know what I wanted to do with my life. I had done work on my Master's, and I considered -- I thought I wanted to go back to school and finish my Master's. And the hospital called me.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: This is the one you worked at before?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, it was -- I had gone from Hahnemann Hospital to Mt. Zion Hospital when I came back from Delaware. And I taught nutrition, diet therapy, for the student nurses for the affiliates from the University of California dietetics program, and when they had a service for Mt. Zion, and so they kept calling me to come to work, back to work. And that was an interesting transition in that they had been noted prior to the war for their wonderful food and beautiful service in their hospital. And, of course, war years took its toll with what was -- they were able to serve and the type of help that you had because people went to work for the shipyards and they didn't want to work for minimum pay. So it was difficult to find help and that sort of thing. But I worked long hours. It was a lot of hard work in that to be responsible for lectures and labs and at that point you did rounds with the doctors. And so that it was a long time, long days. But that's all I had to do. I didn't -- I wasn't thinking of the future.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. Let's go back to Europe and World War II a bit. What was some of the toughest decisions you had to make or any incidents that scared you or stand out as really key incidents?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Oh, what might be considered frivolous things now, you know, were you remember those things where you just took -- Well, it was probably making sure that everybody got fed and what they were supposed to -- how they were supposed to be taken care of. And it was difficult to see the damage that had been done to the communities and the landscape and the things we had to work with. There were not electric hot carts to keep food warm in transport from, you know, maybe a block away to buildings that were not heated properly. And we sent our food in what they called drinking water boxes. They were metal-lined wooden boxes like a foot locker, and we'd put boiling water in and these canisters of food and hope that they might be tepid by the time the patients got them. Most of the patients -- a lot of the patients were ambulatory, and we did have a nice -- we sanded our tables ourselves, and they used to issue lemon powder, and we made a solution of the lemon powder and it really bleached those tables, and then we sort of scrounged some shellac, and our tables looked pretty nice. And we scrounged some materials and made curtains. So our mess hall looked nice for the men.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How much with the wounded -- Here again back in Europe. Of the wounded, how much time did you spend just being a listener to the soldiers?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Lots of time. And not only to the patients but to the cadre. We knew every family. Every time anyone got a picture of a girl friend or baby or whatever, they'd come and our coffeepot was going all the time.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So as one of the few women, you realized the importance of the American woman to the American man, right?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum. We were friends to all of them. I can recall many -- most of the names.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Did you -- were there any patients that were in really bad shape that you recall?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yes. Oh, yes. There were a lot of burn cases, and they treated them as they knew how then, but it was -- those probably were the hardest because feeding them was a problem, and they were encased with bandages and not open like it was in Korea.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: When you lost a patient, how did that hit you?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Oh, always hard. Most of -- Well, I probably didn't have a lot of association with that except just to know they were no longer there, and the most serious were evacuated as soon as they could be to England usually.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. Okay. So let's go forward again to we're in 1946, you're working at a hospital in Oakland.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No. San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: In San Francisco. What happened to this lieutenant from Salzburg?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Did you have his address when you left?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Oh, sure. We corresponded occasionally, but the letters were sort of few and far between. So when I -- I finally decided that I would go back to school, but in the meantime -- I guess prior to that -- I'm just trying to think. Prior to my going back to the hospital I was -- right after I was discharged I was contacted by the Air Transport Command and offered a job as an instructor for an in-flight feeding program. The Air Corps in their air transport system, they wanted to put in-flight feeding in and hot meals. So they sent cooks from all over the country and the world to Stockton. I went to Stockton, California, and this school was established. There was a captain and two sergeants and myself. And I was supposed to give the lectures and instruct, along with the two sergeants, the cooking process. And so from Stockton it was -- they transferred the whole school to -- Leonard Morley: Topeka.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: -- Topeka, Kansas. And I was giving a lecture one morning, 8:00, and the back -- it was an old, you know, building from World War II, and the door opened and here was this lieutenant in a class A uniform, and this was summer now, sharp as a tack, and I let out this squeal, and that was Len. So his excuse was that he had a sister-in-law living in Topeka, his brother was in Salina, and he had just came to visit them, but he had called my home and found I was in Topeka.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You didn't believe him, did you?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, I knew he had called my father, you know. We picnicked and I took the day off, that day off, and went to movies and danced, but that was all. We were friends. We were good friends, and there were big shoes to fill in my life.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: So he only wore 8 1/2, and Nels' (phonetic) shoes had been about a 12 I suppose. So anyhow, and I still had thoughts of going back to school. Then I went back to -- That sort of folded up, and they wanted me to go to Washington, and I didn't want to go to Washington, D.C. And I went back to San Francisco, and that's when I went back to the hospital. And so at the end of that year I kept telling them that I didn't want to stay because of the situation there, and so I quit my job.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Now, this is the end of '47?

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: It was in June -- the spring of '47.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And I had quit my job, and I hadn't decided where I wanted to go back -- where I wanted to go to school. And I got a postcard from Len from New York saying he was coming home on leave, and that he was picking up a car in Oklahoma. Leonard Morley: Convertible, yet.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And that he'd stop and see me. So he stopped and we visited, and that was all. And when he left I said Well, that's probably the end I'll ever see of him, and that was -- Leonard Morley: I went to Seattle.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: He went to Seattle, but he left his shirt -- a shirt at our house, and he wrote me a note and said I'm coming by to pick up my shirt before I go to Fort Lee. And at that point we talked and decided that maybe our lives, we'd be well to join forces. And so we went to see my parents to tell them, and my mother who was -- she had a sense of humor, and we told them that we were going to be married, and my mother went around to Len and she put her arms around him and she said You're an answer to prayer, and Len has never let me forget it.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Did he sing for her? Okay. So you have convinced your mother that you and Len are going to get married, and you're going to go to Fort Lee, correct?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: 1947, and where did you get married?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Chapel number 1.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Chapel number 1.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: In Fort Lee. It was an old-style chapel.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: All right. Was your whole family there or who was there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I was just there.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Just you?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And you told me earlier, tell me about your plans for your wedding and what you had to do about buying dresses.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, I had not planned for a formal wedding, and I had gotten probably the most expensive dress I had ever owned at Magnin's in San Francisco. And I went to Bismarck, North Dakota to visit my sister on the way, and I had a note from Len, I hope you don't mind, it's going to be formal. I was not prepared for that. So finding a dress in Mandan, North Dakota and shoes in Chicago and arriving in Richmond and meeting -- I had purchased a dress for the bridesmaid or matron of honor and not knowing her size or anything, but I bought it so it would fit me if she didn't want to use it. And we got married and celebrated with a wedding cake with blue frosting, infantry blue.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Infantry blue frosting. At the Officers Club.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That sounds like something Len Morley would do. Okay. So we go forward. So it's 1947 now, October 10th.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: 10th.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: 1947. You get married. And how long are you stationed at Fort Lee?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Until July of '48.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: July of '48. Where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: To Monterey for the language school.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you're back in the general area of California, so you're closer to family, and how long were you -- a year there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: A year.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. 1949 now. What's happening then?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Len went to Japan in the summer, in July or August of '48 -- I mean '49. Pardon me. And I followed in December.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: December '49. What -- what was Japan like? Was there still stuff left over? I remember as a kid in 1949 if it said Made in Japan, it meant junk. Was Japan still a war zone?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: It was quite a drive from Yoko --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yokohama.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: -- Yokohama to Tokyo, with seeing the damage, and we were in Tokyo. We lived -- our first apartment there was not in the temporary billets but the first apartment was in the old war ministry buildings, and it was called Pershing Heights. Leonard Morley: Three rooms.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: One bedroom, one small kitchen, one bathroom, but we had got as part of the reparations that Japan owed the United States, you were given -- I don't mean given but a servant to help you depending on the size of your quarters, and we had a delightful young lady by the name of Shasui Song (phonetic), and she was a treasure.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How long was -- How did Japan compare to what you saw in Europe as far as devastation?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, where we were it was probably equal to Frankfurt and Munich.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So now you're sitting there in -- you're in Tokyo.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And what are you doing during this time? Len's working in the military, and what are you doing?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, I played golf. No. Time was busy, and we learned all about the city. There were not a lot of cars. There were bicycles, and the Japanese cars were fueled by charcoal burners, and there were still rickshaws. And so we scoured the countryside on our time off until June.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: June 1950. Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, we were -- had gone -- It was on a Sunday. We had gone to friends of ours, Colonel and Mrs. Knox, Cameron Knox, and he was a radio ham, and Len was going to help him put up his antenna. Of course, in Japan most stores and shops and things were open seven days a week, 24 hours a day practically. And so Helen and I were designated to go and pick up some lumber at the lumberyard, and when we returned, Cameron was gone, and we waited all day to hear from him. About 5:00 he came in and changed his uniform and picked up some extra uniforms and away he went. He was on the staff of General MacArthur. And as Len had been incommunicado with his office, he was with the foreign liaison office, we got back, and then I went to work for Special Services. Everybody needed help in the office, and then they needed help at the hospital. So December of '40 -- of '50 I was -- Leonard Morley: Recalled.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Went on active duty.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Did you volunteer or did they call you?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No. I volunteered.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So December 1950 the Korean War is going on. It's not going well for us.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And was there any fear in Japan that they were going to come across and hit Japan or did you feel like it was contained to Korea?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I don't think we had a fear then. Some families -- I mean men who had families there sent their families home, but I certainly had no fear.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Because I had a critical MOS, I could ask for a specific tour, which I asked for one year.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So you had a one-year tour, and you're back again as a dietitian now, correct?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum. Tokyo Army Hospital.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Tokyo Army Hospital.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Worked with two fabulous gals that both became chief of the Medical Specialist Corps in future years, Mary Lipscomb and June Williams.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Have you stayed in touch with them?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Mary has passed away, and June I haven't been recently in touch with her, but anyhow...

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Was your job there pretty much like it was in Europe during World War II?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No. It was entirely different. The hospital was in a beautiful establishment that was built by the Episcopal Church, St. Luke's, but we -- it was certainly we had patients in the halls and wards were crowded and injuries were entirely different, burn cases, lots of hand-to-hand combat. We had nurses and doctors from all the United Nations countries. And patients, the Greeks and the Turks and the Australians. I mean, there were all these nations that were part of the United --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You had language problems as well as the different kinds of wounds?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, yes. One of the things that was sort of fun at the time because of the Turks and the Greeks, particularly the Turks, they don't eat pork. So when pork was on the menu, we got a substitute. But we also had a butcher, and we cut our own bacon and -- cut our own meat for the hospital, had a beautiful kitchen, and all our help though was Japanese. And we'd slice our own bacon, but they'd take the rind and roll it and then slice it and we'd make cracklins out of it, and that was sort of a specialty that was put on the line. And we tried in every way possible to make sure that there was a sign that it was forbidden for the Turks particularly, and that was their favorite food. Also they liked what we'd class as yogurt today but it was a clabber of milk and, of course, we used reconstituted milk, and it didn't make very good clabber. Clabber, that was the old-fashioned term. But anyhow, they were making an inspection of the annex one day where there were a lot of orthopedic patients, and they were up and out of their beds and wandering around, but they couldn't figure out what the odor was. And the patients had instituted a system where they could start on the windowsill which was usually above the heater, and they would have rows of the cartons of milk, and by the time it got to the end, it was the proper consistency. But because we used a rennet tablet to make that for seriously ill patients, we just couldn't do it for everybody, and that was quite an innervation that the patients had.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So how long were you in this hospital? How long did you work there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I worked there for the year, and then I replaced myself as a civilian for six months.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you came back. So by now we're up to what, 19 --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: '52. The war is still going on.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yes. And we came home.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You came home. Len got transferred, and you came back. Where did you come to from there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Washington, D.C.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: What was your -- what was your view of the Korean War versus World War II? Was it pretty much the same feelings or what?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yes. We were -- and we were busy, very busy in the hospital. Our commander was Kenneth Brewer and our chief nurse was Colonel Galloway. Wasn't that right? Leonard Morley: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And we had an interesting time. That was at the time when General MacArthur was relieved, and that was another important time.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How was -- how did that impact you? What was the feeling of the troops when that happened?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, it was -- it impacted us as such because Len was sent to the embassy the next day to coordinate all the travel and packing and travel of the whole staff and was able to meet with Mrs. MacArthur, and the General came down for lunch. And as Len had served in the 42nd Division in World War II, and he had command of the division in World War I, he spotted Len's patch, and Len came home that evening with Would you like to shake the hand of... But in any case, it was -- I have pictures and the newspaper articles that show the mass of people that lined the highway or the road to Onetta, the air base where he left from.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So MacArthur was well loved by the Japanese.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: He innovated the beginning of their economy of today because he insisted that there was not the shoddy manufacturing of products, that they had quality control for their manufacturing, and I think that they would never forget that.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Did you ever meet Deming when he came, when MacArthur brought him over there as a quality guy?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. Okay. So 1952. You come back to the States. You go to the Pentagon. Is that your next assignment?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Len went there.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Len went there, and you're out there, you're a civilian, so you're back to not working.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Being a housewife.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So you go forward. Give me a quick run-through through the '50s and we're going to go back up to the middle of '65.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, the '50s, we left the tour in the Pentagon, and from there we went to Fort Benning where Len attended the advanced class and went to Airborne, and from there we were on orders to go to Fort Carson which was Camp Carson then and joined the 8th Division. But in the meantime we were on temporary duty at Camp McCoy, Wisconsin for the summer. And so after 19 months of TDY from Washington to Colorado Springs, that was a long time, and from Colorado Springs we went to Europe on the Gyro movement which was where they exchanged the whole division from stateside, from Europe, and when you landed in Europe --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That's with the 8th Division?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: 8th Division.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: In what year was that?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: We went over in '56.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. How was Europe in 1956 compared to when you left there in 1946?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Depended on where you were, who had been in the zones, like the French zone or the British zone or the American zone. And we went from Fort Carson to Nuremberg, and that was a pleasant assignment. Of course, after we were together for so long, this whole group of people, and we went on the advanced party and came back with the last of them, of that unit, and they were battle groups instead of regimens. And we were close-knit. The men were in the field a lot, so there were a lot of -- I made many trips to the hospital for skinned knees and broken arms and new babies.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Now, you are -- At this time is he captain or major?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Was a captain I guess, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you're looking out for your lieutenants and sergeants and privates and looking out for the families of the unit, is that correct?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you were over there how long?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Almost three years. So that puts you --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Three years.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Came back in '59.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: '59. Where did you go?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Fort Riley.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Fort Riley. 1st Division then? Were they there then? Leonard Morley: Yes. Figurehead 1.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Figurehead 1. Okay. How long were you in Fort Riley?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Six months.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Six months. And then where did you go?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Fort Leavenworth.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. What did you do at Leavenworth? Command and General Staff? Leonard Morley: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. For another year, nine months?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Year.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Year. Okay. Then where?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: From there Len went to Korea.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Korea. And you stayed home. Where did you stay?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Oakland.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Oakland. Went back home, okay. So you spent a year -- Len's not here. We're talking to you. Okay. So you went to Korea for a year, so now we're up to what, '61?

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: '61. Then where did you go?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Went back to Washington, D.C.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Pentagon. Okay. Any thoughts about that?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: That was an interesting time. General MacArthur died, and because of the association with the 42nd Division we were, that unit, the retirees in the whole Washington, D.C. area, we were part of the wreath laying at the Rotunda at the Capitol, and it was in the evening, and it was a beautiful -- It's hard to describe what that Rotunda looked like in the dim light and as they laid the wreath. We were there when the President was -- President Kennedy was assassinated, when General Eisenhower became president, so...

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you've had some good experiences in Washington, D.C.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yes. It's a place where I would not want to retire there, but if you're stationed there, it's a learning of history. You feel the pulse of the nation that you don't feel anywhere else in the nation.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So from Washington, D.C. on that tour, where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Oh, dear.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Are we up to '63 or '64 now?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Oh, we came to Fort Lewis.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Fort Lewis. And what was your first job at Fort Lewis?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Finding a place to live. No. We had temporary sort of quarters. And then Len was promoted to colonel, and we got to move, and we were there until the unit went to Vietnam. Leonard Morley: Well, I was promoted before we went to Fort Lewis.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No, not to colonel.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So we have -- Let's talk about so far you've always lived in temporary quarters. When did you buy your first house? Did you buy it at Fort Lewis?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No. At the language school.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: The language school.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: It was a shack.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. And did you sell it or did you hold onto it?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, we paid $5,200 for it on an unpaved street, no sidewalks, everybody used the backyard for a dump, and we made a little dollhouse. But at the end of that year, see, there was nothing to rent that we could afford. And at the end of the year there were four-bedroom ranch houses for nothing down, and so finding a buyer was difficult. And we had had to pay 50 percent of that when we bought it, and that was not easy.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: But Len went to Japan, and I stayed, and I got it sold to a young Coast Guard couple, and they paid me -- Leonard Morley: She sold it on a conditional sales contract.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: -- $100 down or something like that, and they lived in it the three years we were in Japan, and then they asked if they could sell it, and we said yes. So I bought my first freezer when we sold the property.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So you got to Fort Lewis. Did you buy a house out there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Eventually. We lived on post.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Eventually, okay. So we go forward to 19 -- you took -- Let's see. Len took command of the battalion in 1965, is that right, in January?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: January 1965. And this is an unusual interview as we talk to historians in the future because I then joined you in Thanksgiving of 1965, and at that time the battalion was well under strength and we had very few people. We were on Task Force ACE which was a ready reaction force, and we had to fill with filler personnel. And then you knew before we did, but when did you find out about the mission that we were getting ready to pick up through trained troops and go to Vietnam?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I don't -- I just -- I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Len and I never discussed.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. You didn't discuss it. Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And also we didn't discuss personalities, and I think that's important for people to realize that he didn't want to hear anything I heard over a bridge table or from the chatter of women about family affairs that I might have heard, and he said I cannot make decisions about men if I have to think about something that happens within a private home.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That's very interesting. That's very interesting.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And so we never really discussed personalities or duty.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So how did you learn to be a colonel's wife? Was there any education or just osmosis?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Just osmosis.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. Because --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: And when I had to have my first coffee and I didn't -- I didn't have enough china to serve, but I never -- That's something I tried to teach, not teach but show the younger women that they didn't have to put on airs. You use what you had, and you were yourself in your own home. And we were -- as long as your house was clean and you could borrow from your neighbor, you could do all sorts of things, and you didn't have to put on a show for anyone. You could be yourself.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Back then very few of the wives worked. We had lots of lieutenants fresh out of college, freshly married within the previous year or so, some captains, and of course we had a couple of majors, but let's focus on the lieutenants and the captains. Did you feel it was your responsibility to train those wives to be Army wives, to be officers' wives?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: But you did such a good job of it, that just sort of came just because it was the right thing to do?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, I think if you're yourself and people observe you, and you can say you don't have to put on an air. You can be yourself and be kind to one another. And something my mother taught me, never say anything that you would ever regret. If you can't say something nice, just don't say it.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Because as a young lieutenant with a young wife in your battalion, I always felt that you and Len had a plan, that you were to train the wives and he was to train the soldiers, but you're telling me that you just did it.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I just did it.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And you didn't talk about it.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So what -- what Phyllis said in -- she never turned around and said this is what's going on at the Babcock household.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Indeed not.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: All right. Very interesting. Okay. Leonard Morley: She never turned in any lesson plans.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So then we get troops fresh in January of 1966, and we get busy as the dickens. So what tempo did you feel changed there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, I tried to have meals on time. And it became evident that you were going to be going overseas, and I think that by just being myself, that was all I could do.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay. So was there ever any talking and planning between you and Sergeant Major Aruda's (phonetic) wife, for instance, about the contingencies when we left, what you were going to do with the families?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No. Probably the realization that a lot of women would be staying, both enlisted families and officers and their families, their wives and their families, and you just sort of stood by, and I answered phone calls. After you left, the phone rang all the time, and there were lots of problems, mainly with men that had been probably counseled -- counseled is wrong -- in that don't sign power of attorney to your wives, don't send allotments. I mean, there was a limited amount of money for families. And as in all families, it doesn't matter whether military or not, young people, children get in trouble, and so there were lots of little things, and women would call. One thing I never did, if there was really serious problems, I said I don't want to know your name. Tell me your problem. I'll see what I can do to find the answer. You call me back. I will remember. And that way it would never be said that Mrs. Morley said this and Mrs. Morley said that and, you know, I was just someone that was trying to help. I was called quite a few times when there was the death of a soldier, to go with the chaplain. And this was hard but, again, you just take each day as it came. We had --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I worked with -- One of the things that took a lot of time and several wives, we had gotten together when we first went to Fort Lewis and established a loan closet, and at that time there were lots of shirts to iron, and everybody when they came they didn't have their ironing boards and irons, and the prisoners at the prison on post would repair the irons. Cribs needed screws and things. I got to know the Salvation Army and all the service organizations, and I could go and pick out what I needed. And there were some wholesale places that I bought ironing boards. We'd have donations, and I could sell what we didn't use at the loan closet, through the thrift shop, and get money to buy ironing board covers and ironing boards. I think we had 100 ironing boards at one time. But people would unpack, and they'd have extra dishes they didn't want. We took anything and established and probably could -- and families would be burned out. I took sheets and blankets to families.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: But this is just something you did. Nobody told you to do it.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: You just did it because it was the right thing to do.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: You just did it, and I wasn't the only one. There were lots of women that did that.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: That's the nice part about the Army family, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum. It is. You take care of each other.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Yeah. That's the thing in my short time I learned the most. I mean, the Army takes care of itself. Let's back up before we go to Vietnam. Did you get many of the wives coming to you with concerns before we embarked for Vietnam? Because we were in the field all the time, and they had lots of time by themselves.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I think so. Probably they didn't come to me as such but, you know, we had children born, we had showers, we had -- there was families had problems with quite a few things. But again, they could be solved.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: So let's fast forward to, let's see, Len left on advanced party, but then on July 21st of 1966 his unit left.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And we left on the Nelson Walker, and I never will forget you down there on the dock with your -- with some of the wives and a sign that says They're off, the regulars, by God. What were your feelings that day? You've been through two wars now. What -- you know, we're going off to another one, and you're staying home. What did you think about that?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, it was a sad day, but I couldn't feel the sadness. I had to be strong, I think, but I think we all went to lunch afterwards.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Did you? I always wondered what you did.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I think we went to Johnny Stock and had lunch.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Because as I recall there were probably half a dozen wives that were still there.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: I don't remember exactly.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: I don't remember the number either, but I've got a picture of it, in fact, I took from the ship. I ought to show you all that some day. But so it was kind of an empty feeling for all of us I guess.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yes, it was.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: And you know, the first -- the first casualty, thinking of the officers that were killed, were you involved when Dick Collins was killed? Did you --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Was Linda still up there?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No. She was down --

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: In California?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: No. She was in Oregon. I went to see her. When she had -- She was pregnant I think, and she had a baby, and I went to see her. So unfortunately, I didn't keep in touch with her at that point after that. She seemed to be taken care of, you know, being taken care of.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: But just on your own you felt it was your --

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Then I went to California, there were several that lived down around Fresno, and I had taken my mother to California for a trip. So I took a day and drove from San Jose to Fresno and had lunch with them.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Umhum. Okay. So any other things that come to mind about while we're in Vietnam that stick out with you: good, bad or indifferent?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Well, of course, we all waited for letters, and there were things that happened. One particular incident, the son of one of our friends was killed his last day of work, he was a junior at Washington State, and he was killed, and it shows how Army wives could stick together. And the younger son -- younger brother of the young man that was killed called and said Mother needs you, and I had just gotten home and changed into my gardening clothes, and I told my mother I'd be back, and by the time I got there her former neighbor had been there. I called the chaplain, chaplain -- I'm not sure which chaplain it was. And Mrs. Beyers, General Beyers' wife was there. And the husband, the father, that was on a Friday, and I met him at Seatac on Sunday morning. He was in the jungle. Leonard Morley: It was George Wilcox.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: George Wilcox.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Wilcox, I'll be darn. I didn't know about that. He was the XO at the brigade, right? Leonard Morley: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: That was -- that was hard.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: How about General Collins' wife, did she have an involvement during this time?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Yes. She didn't stay here that long, I mean in the area, but General Collins' wife was active, and Mrs. Beyers, and there weren't too many senior women that stayed in the area.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Right. So fast forward till early summer of '67 and Len came home when? June?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: June.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Something like that? Yeah. And where did you meet him? Did he fly back to Tacoma?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: McChord.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: McChord. Okay. And then what was your next assignment after that?

sp.speaker: Chartley M. Morley
sp.p: Fort Leavenworth.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
sp.p: Fort Leavenworth, the Command and General Staff as a -- Leonard Morley: Staff faculty.

sp.speaker: Robert Babcock
